Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

our club’s Wednesday evening run is meant to be predictable, but the route sometimes needs changing when there is a problem on the river path. this note explains how we make that change without leaving anyone to discover it halfway through a run. Northbank Striders has about forty-two people on its weekly email list, though attendance changes from week to week. The usual meeting point is the west entrance of Alder Park, at 6:15 p.m. We have three pace groups, and the run is intended to finish at the same entrance by 7:30.

The route lead checks the riverside path before lunch on Wednesday, using the city parks notice page and, when needed, a short walk past the affected section. A closure sign is not the only thing that matters. The lead also checks for standing water, fallen branches, poor lighting, or construction equipment that could make the path awkward for a group. If a hazard is only near one part of the route, the whole run still changes; splitting the club around it would make it harder to account for people.

There are two regular alternatives. The first goes through Alder Park and loops around the library and the old mill, then returns by Maple Street. It is 4.8 kilometres, mostly paved, with one narrow crossing at the library driveway. The second is a 6.2-kilometre loop using Cedar Avenue and the school track. The track is open to the public after 5:30, but school events can make it unavailable, so the route lead checks the school calendar as well. Neither alternative is automatically better: the shorter one has more turns, while the longer one has a hill on Cedar Avenue.

1. The decision and notice

By 2 p.m., the route lead tells the club coordinator whether the river path is usable. If the information is uncertain, the lead says that directly rather than treating a guess as a confirmed closure. The coordinator posts the route choice in the club’s email group and on the notice board at Alder Park. A usual message says, “Tonight we’ll use the library loop; the riverside path has standing water near the footbridge.” If the route is still being checked, the message says when an update will come, usually by 4:30 p.m.

The notice gives the distance, meeting point, expected finish time, and any feature that could affect the group, such as the Cedar Avenue hill or the narrow driveway crossing. It also says whether the route is suitable for the run-walk group. We do not assume that a person who misses the email will see a social media post, so the coordinator asks the route lead to bring a printed copy. The copy is placed beside the sign-in sheet, not on the park gate, where it could be mistaken for a city notice.

2. On the evening

The route lead arrives by 6 p.m. and checks that the printed notice matches the latest message. If conditions have changed, the lead contacts the coordinator and asks for a correction before people begin gathering. The lead does not quietly change the route at the start line and expect everyone to hear about it. At 6:10, the three pace leaders review the route, the regrouping points, and who is carrying the small first-aid pouch. Each group has a named leader, and the pace leaders confirm they have the current route on their phones or on paper.

At the start, the coordinator gives a short explanation to the whole club. “We’re taking the library loop tonight. Please wait at the library driveway crossing until your leader has counted the group.” People who arrive after the briefing can check the printed notice and ask the coordinator. A late runner is not sent after a group without first being told which route it took. If a person needs the run-walk option, the coordinator points out that its leader is using the same loop and will regroup at the library entrance.

The leaders count their runners before leaving Alder Park, at the library, and when they return. They do not need to keep the groups together at every step, but they wait at the stated points so a runner can rejoin after slowing down. If someone is missing at a count, the leader checks with the other pace leaders and contacts the coordinator before anyone searches alone. The coordinator stays at the meeting point until all three groups return or a leader has confirmed a different arrangement.

After the run, the route lead makes a brief note of the route used, the reason for any change, and any problem noticed on the alternative. For example, a report that the library driveway was difficult to cross may lead us to use the school-track loop next week, if the track is available. These notes are kept in the club’s shared folder, with the date in the file name, so the next route lead can find them. The note is not treated as a promise that the same route will be used again; conditions and school events may be different. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "last thursday i went to the cedar loop running club's monthly meeting, which was in the back room at miller's grocery, the room they rent on the second floor. i got there around six twenty, even though the meeting was supposed to start at six thirty, and there were already nine people there, with coats over the backs of chairs and shoes lined up beside the radiator. the club keeps a sign-in sheet on a clipboard by the door. i wrote my name and the distance i usually run, which is about three miles, though some weeks it's less. the room smelled like coffee and wet wool because it had been raining since midafternoon. marisol, who runs the club's beginner group, brought a tin of lemon cookies and said, “they're a little cracked, but they taste fine.”

we sat around two folding tables pushed into a square, except one table had a leg that kept shifting if somebody leaned on it. caleb put a paperback map of the river path in the middle, with a few corners folded over and pencil marks near the footbridge. he said he'd walked the route on sunday, not run it, because the north entrance was muddy. the group spent a while trying to remember whether the path lights stay on past eight. no one seemed certain, and priya said she'd check with the parks office before the saturday run. that was one of the things we talked about, but not the only reason for the meeting. the main topic was how the club should arrange its spring runs, and which ones could include people who don't want to go fast.

1. spring schedule and meeting points
we looked at the calendar that nora printed out, with march, april and may on separate pages. the first run she had put down was march twenty-third, meeting at the library steps at eight in the morning. she thought the route might be four miles, but said that could change after somebody checks the construction work by oak street. then she mentioned a shorter route on april sixth, starting outside the pool, and a longer one on april twentieth that would use the river path. nobody voted on the dates, and nora asked people to email her if they saw a conflict. she also asked if we could avoid putting every start at the library, since the number 14 bus doesn't stop nearby on weekends. people offered the pool entrance and the west lot at cedar park as alternatives. there wasn't a decision about the meeting places.

2. the pace groups
marisol said the beginner group has had a bigger turnout lately, usually six or seven people, but that the range in pace is wider than she can manage while also watching the route. she asked if another club member could come along on some weeks. dan said, “i can do two saturdays in april, but i can't promise every week.” he works early shifts and has his schedule only a month ahead. jo offered to take the back of the group for the march run, if the route stays near three miles. nobody said the club was starting a new program; they were talking about ways to share the work. someone suggested that runners write their usual distance on the sign-up sheet, though marisol said pace mattered more than distance when people are choosing a group. we didn't settle which information to add.

3. equipment and practical details
caleb passed around a small hand lamp he bought for running at dusk. it had a red setting as well as a white one, and he said the battery lasted longer on red, but he hadn't tested that claim on a full run. tessa asked whether club members were expected to bring their own lights for the march evening run. the club doesn't have equipment to lend, as far as i know, and nobody offered to buy any. they talked about making a list of local places that sell reflective bands, but that was an idea rather than an assignment. nora wrote “check visibility” in the margin of the calendar and drew a box around it. she also asked everyone to tell her if they wanted a printed copy of the route notes, because some people prefer a paper map to looking at a phone while they're outside.

after that, people ate cookies and talked in smaller groups. i asked priya about the saturday run, and she said it would probably be easy pace, but she hadn't decided the route yet. she was thinking about starting at cedar park, then going toward the footbridge if the ground wasn't too slick. i said i might come, but i would check the weather in the morning first. the meeting ended a little after seven thirty. we folded the tables, put the chairs against the wall, and left the sign-in clipboard on the shelf by the door. i left with a photocopy of nora's calendar and two cookies in a paper napkin; the march dates were written on it, but the meeting places were still open questions.", "output": "Last Thursday, I went to the Cedar Loop Running Club's monthly meeting in the back room at Miller's Grocery, which the club rents on the second floor. I arrived around 6:20, although the meeting was supposed to start at 6:30. Nine people were already there, with coats draped over chair backs and shoes lined up beside the radiator. The club keeps a sign-in sheet on a clipboard by the door. I wrote my name and my usual running distance, about three miles, though some weeks I run less. The room smelled of coffee and wet wool because it had been raining since midafternoon. Marisol, who leads the club's beginner group, brought a tin of lemon cookies and said, “They're a little cracked, but they taste fine.”

We sat around two folding tables pushed together in a square, though one table had a leg that kept shifting whenever someone leaned on it. Caleb placed a paperback map of the river path in the middle, its corners folded and pencil marks clustered near the footbridge. He said he'd walked the route on Sunday, rather than run it, because the north entrance was muddy. For a while, the group tried to remember whether the path lights stay on past eight. No one seemed certain, and Priya said she'd check with the parks office before the Saturday run. That was one of the topics, but not the meeting's only purpose. The main discussion was how to arrange the club's spring runs and which ones could include people who don't want to go fast.

1. Spring schedule and meeting points

We looked at the calendar Nora had printed, with March, April, and May on separate pages. The first run listed was March 23, with a meeting at the library steps at 8:00 in the morning. Nora thought the route might be four miles, but said that could change once someone checked on the construction work near Oak Street. She then mentioned a shorter route on April 6, starting outside the pool, and a longer one on April 20 that would use the river path. No one voted on the dates, and Nora asked people to email her if they spotted a conflict. She also asked whether we could avoid starting every run at the library, since the number 14 bus doesn't stop nearby on weekends. People suggested the pool entrance and the west lot at Cedar Park as alternatives. The meeting places remained undecided.

2. The pace groups

Marisol said the beginner group had drawn a larger turnout lately, usually six or seven people, but the range of paces was wider than she could manage while also watching the route. She asked whether another club member could come along some weeks. Dan said, “I can do two Saturdays in April, but I can't promise every week.” He works early shifts and only gets his schedule a month ahead. Jo offered to bring up the rear of the group for the March run, if the route stayed close to three miles. No one said the club was starting a new program; they were discussing ways to share the work. Someone suggested that runners write their usual distance on the sign-up sheet, though Marisol said pace mattered more than distance when people were choosing a group. We didn't decide what information to add.

3. Equipment and practical details

Caleb passed around a small hand lamp he'd bought for running at dusk. It had a red setting as well as a white one. He said the battery lasted longer on red, but he hadn't tested that claim over a full run. Tessa asked whether club members were expected to bring their own lights for the March evening run. As far as I know, the club doesn't have equipment to lend, and no one offered to buy any. They discussed making a list of local places that sell reflective bands, but that was an idea, not an assignment. Nora wrote “check visibility” in the calendar's margin and drew a box around it. She also asked everyone to tell her if they wanted printed route notes, since some people prefer a paper map to looking at a phone while outside.

Afterward, people ate cookies and talked in smaller groups. I asked Priya about the Saturday run. She said it would probably be at an easy pace, but she hadn't decided on the route yet. She was considering starting at Cedar Park and heading toward the footbridge if the ground wasn't too slick. I said I might come, but would check the weather in the morning first. The meeting ended a little after 7:30. We folded the tables, put the chairs against the wall, and left the sign-in clipboard on the shelf by the door. I left with a photocopy of Nora's calendar and two cookies wrapped in a paper napkin. The March dates were written on it, but the meeting places were still open questions."}, {"id": "arka-v3-train-polish-0106", "row_sha256": "af3c13aacfe2ee6141e4b218c08eaa3c627fd8c4c98bda27062d9ec08b4a1fc6", "mode": "/polish", "language": "en", "context": {"profile": "Plain and direct."}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Rewrite awkward phrasing into readable prose for the supplied profile, or plain prose when none is supplied.
